statement: The title is under 12 words and states the finding, not the topic: "We cut cold starts by 70% by deleting a cache", not "Thoughts on caching".
Under the title put a one-line dek in italics, a single sentence that tells a busy reader whether to keep going.
Open with the problem as someone actually hit it, in the first paragraph, with the real number that made it hurt.
No "In this post I will". Never open with a dictionary definition or with history.
The intro has no heading of its own; the first headed section after it is The Problem.
Sections go in this order: The Problem, What We Tried, What Worked, The Numbers, What I'd Do Differently, Takeaways. Takeaways is always last.
Paragraphs run 2 to 4 sentences. A one-sentence paragraph is allowed once per post, for the line I most want remembered.
What We Tried lists the dead ends as a numbered list, at least two of them, each with why it failed in a clause.
Be honest about the dead ends: include the one that makes me look slow.
Include exactly one code block, under What Worked, no longer than 15 lines, and it must be code that actually ran.
Give the code block a language tag and introduce it with a sentence ending in a colon.
Three to five rows in that table, and every figure carries its unit.
Every number in the prose must match the table to the digit; never round one and not the other.
State how the measurements were taken (tool, sample, period) in one sentence right below the table.
Don't claim more than the data shows; if it was one service over a couple of weeks, say so.
Write "I" for what I did and "we" for what the team did, and don't swap them carelessly.
Name tools, libraries and versions exactly: "Postgres 15.4", not "a recent Postgres".
Each section except Takeaways opens with a sentence that could stand alone as its summary.
What I'd Do Differently is one paragraph, no more than 80 words, and it names at least one specific mistake of mine.
Takeaways is a bulleted list of exactly three bullets, each under 20 words.
Each takeaway should be usable by someone who doesn't run our stack; if it only applies to us it's not a takeaway.
No exclamation marks anywhere.
Use at most one analogy in the whole post, and only if it carries weight a plain statement couldn't.
Headings in Title Case, no more than five words each, and never phrased as a question.
Put the single most important number in the first 100 words.
Explain a term the first time it shows up if a mid-level engineer from another specialty might not know it.
Keep sentences under 28 words; split anything longer.
Say what the fix cost in time, money or complexity. A win with no price is an advert.
Don't hedge with "might possibly" or "somewhat"; say what I know and mark a guess with "my guess is".
Write file names, commands and config keys in backticks, exactly as they'd be typed.
End the post on the last takeaway bullet: no sign-off, no "thanks for reading", no call to subscribe.
Give dates and durations precisely, "over 9 days in March", rather than "recently" or "for a while".
Cut any paragraph that only tells the reader how to feel about the next paragraph.
No bold for emphasis in body text; if a sentence needs bold it needs rewriting.
Read it aloud once; anything I wouldn't say to a colleague across a desk gets rewritten.
Make the reader able to reproduce the check, if not the fix: give enough for them to measure the same thing on their own system.
Start with a single line naming the pull request by number and title, exactly as the author titled it.
Put the Verdict section first, before anything else, so nobody has to scroll to find out whether they can merge.
The Verdict is one of: Approve, Request changes, Comment. Write that word in bold and nothing softer.
Follow the verdict word with one sentence giving the reason, and keep that sentence under 30 words.
Second section is Summary: say what the change does in my own words, not the author's description pasted back.
Keep the Summary to one paragraph of at most 4 sentences and make sure it says what changed and why.
Read the whole diff twice before writing a word; the first pass is for understanding, the second for faults.
After Summary the order is Blocking Issues, Non-Blocking Suggestions, Questions, Test Coverage, What Works, and Next Steps last. Never reorder them.
Weigh risk before style: a data-loss bug outranks any number of naming complaints.
Number the blocking issues and limit them to five; if there are more than five the PR needs splitting and I say that instead.
Quote the offending code exactly as it stands in the diff, never paraphrased, in inline code or a fenced block.
For every blocking issue say what breaks, for whom, and under what input; a reviewer who can't name the failure hasn't found one.
Offer a concrete fix for each blocking issue, in a sentence beginning "Suggest:".
Non-Blocking Suggestions is a bulleted list of at most 6 bullets, each a single sentence.
Prefix every non-blocking bullet with "Nit:" or "Consider:" so the author knows how hard I'm pushing.
Never write "just", "simply", "obviously" or "clearly"; what's obvious to me wasn't to the author.
Don't say "you" when describing a fault; talk about the code ("this loop", "the handler"), not the person.
Questions holds real questions only, things I don't know the answer to, each ending with a question mark, and no more than 3 of them.
If there are no questions, keep the heading and write "None." under it. Same for an empty Blocking Issues.
The Covered column takes only Yes, No or Partial.
Put between 3 and 6 rows in the Test Coverage table, and choose the scenarios that would hurt most in production, not the easy ones.
In the Where column name the test file and test function exactly, or write "n/a" when Covered is No.
What Works is short: 2 or 3 bullets naming specific good decisions, never general praise like "nice work".
Refer to the author and other reviewers by handle with an @, spelled as it appears on the PR, and only in What Works or Next Steps.
Next Steps is a numbered list of at most 4 actions, each starting with a verb, ordered by what the author should do first.
The final line of the review says whether I want another look: either "Re-review needed: yes" or "Re-review needed: no".
The whole review stays under 500 words; if it's running long I'm reviewing style instead of substance.
Any figure I quote, a timeout, a retry count, a benchmark number, must match the diff or the PR description to the digit.
Check the change against what the linked ticket asked for, and name the ticket by its ID in the Summary.
Don't ask for a refactor the PR didn't set out to do; if it's worth doing, say it's a follow-up.
Distinguish what I verified by running it from what I only read, and use the phrase "I ran" only when I did.
One issue per numbered item; don't bundle two faults because they sit in the same file.
Bold a short name for each blocking issue at the start of its item, 6 words at most.
No headings below ##; if I need a third level, the review is too tangled.
Assume the author had a reason: when a choice looks odd, ask in Questions before condemning it in Blocking Issues.
Keep every sentence under 30 words.
Use backticks for every identifier, function, file and flag name, spelled as in the code.
Before posting, reread the verdict against the issues list: Approve with open blocking issues is a contradiction, and Request changes with none is a mood.
Head the document with the title "Term Summary:" followed by the deal name in the form the term sheet uses.
Under the title, before section 1, add a one-line italic status marker, and the status is one of: Draft, For Review, Agreed.
Give each party a short name in bold and quote marks on first mention, then use only that short name afterwards.
Never write "the Company" for either side in a mutual document; it invites a fight about who is meant.
Sections run in this order: Parties, Purpose, Key Terms, Obligations, Exclusions, Term and Termination, Governing Law, Open Points, Sign-Off.
Number the sections 1 to 9 in their headings, so people can say "see 4" on a call.
Purpose is one sentence of no more than 40 words; it says why information is changing hands and nothing else.
The Term Sheet Ref column cites the term sheet clause for every row in the form "TS cl. 4.2"; no row goes without one.
Carry over every figure from the term sheet unchanged: dates, periods, caps, notice days. Don't turn 24 months into 2 years.
Write money as currency code then figure, "GBP 250,000", and write periods as a numeral with its unit, "30 days".
Between 6 and 9 rows in Key Terms; if I need more, this isn't a short-form deal and I should tell the partner so.
Obligations is a numbered list of no more than 6 items, each one sentence, starting "Each party shall" or "Neither party shall" where the duty is mutual.
Use "shall" for obligations and "may" for permissions; never "will", "must" or "should" in the Obligations section.
Check an obligation is truly mutual before writing "each party"; where the term sheet makes it one-way, name the party who bears it.
Exclusions sets out the carve-outs as lettered sub-items, (a), (b) and so on, four at most, and only the ones the term sheet actually agreed.
Define each capitalised term once, in bold and quote marks where it first appears, and don't capitalise anything I haven't defined.
Don't use "reasonable endeavours", "best endeavours" or "commercially reasonable efforts" unless the term sheet uses those exact words; then quote it and cite the clause.
No "and/or", no "including but not limited to", no "hereinafter", no "witnesseth".
Term and Termination gives the start date, the duration, the survival period and the notice period, in that order, in at most 3 sentences.
Think about the day after termination: who holds what, and is there a duty to return or destroy it within a stated number of days?
Governing Law is one sentence naming the law and the courts, and it says whether jurisdiction is exclusive or non-exclusive.
Put in Open Points anything the term sheet is silent or ambiguous on; never fill a gap quietly with my own preferred wording.
Order the Open Points by how much money or exposure rides on each, biggest first.
Keep Open Points to 5 rows at most, and where there are none write "None identified" under the heading rather than dropping the section.
In the Term Sheet Says column quote the term sheet's wording in quote marks with its clause, or write "Silent".
Sign-Off is three lines: "Drafted by:", "Reviewed by:" and "Term sheet relied on:".
Give the term sheet's version and date in Sign-Off exactly as printed on it, e.g. "v3, 14 May 2025".
The whole summary fits on one page: 350 to 500 words, counting the tables.
Sentences stay under 35 words; a longer sentence in a contract summary is hiding a second obligation.
Don't summarise a term more favourably to our client than the term sheet reads; the summary goes to both sides.
Flag in Open Points any term that looks unenforceable or out of line for the sector, even if both sides have agreed it.
Write dates in full as "1 March 2026", never 01/03/26.
Write "party" and "parties" in lower case.
No adjectives of comfort: drop "robust", "comprehensive", "standard", "customary" and "usual".
Where a number appears in both words and figures in the term sheet and they disagree, use neither and raise it in Open Points.
Read each obligation as the other side's lawyer would, looking for the reading that hurts.
End the document with the sentence "This summary does not create legal relations." on its own line after Sign-Off.
Title the document "Teardown:" plus the rival product's name and the plan tier and version I examined.
Directly under the title put a line starting "Examined:" that gives the date range and how I got access (trial, paid seat, public docs).
Bottom Line states a Threat Level, and it is one of: Low, Moderate, High, Critical. Put the level in bold.
Sections follow in this order: Bottom Line, Who They Sell To, What They Do Well, Where They Fall Short, Pricing, Feature Comparison, Evidence, What We Should Do. What We Should Do goes last.
Who They Sell To opens with a single sentence naming their ideal customer by size, role and trigger event.
What They Do Well gets exactly three bullets; forcing three makes me rank instead of list.
Lead each of those bullets with a bold label of two to four words, then one sentence of evidence I saw myself.
Be fair to the rival: if I can't write What They Do Well with conviction I haven't used the product enough.
Where They Fall Short also gets three bullets in the same format, and each must be something a customer would feel, not an engineering nitpick.
Never use "clunky", "legacy", "outdated", "inferior" or "killer"; describe what happened when I used it.
Don't call them "the competition" or "the enemy"; use their product name every time.
Copy prices from their public pricing page exactly, currency and period included, and note the date I captured them beneath the table.
One row per plan they publish; for an unlisted enterprise tier write "Not published" in Price rather than guessing.
The Edge column takes only: Them, Us, Even.
Six to eight rows in Feature Comparison, chosen from what buyers actually ask about in deals, not from our roadmap.
In the Them and Us cells write a fact of 8 words or fewer, never a tick or a cross.
Don't rig the comparison: at least two rows should show the Edge as Them if that's the truth, and it usually is.
Evidence is a numbered list of 4 to 7 sources, each saying what it is, where it came from and the date.
Quote customers and reviews word for word in quote marks, with the reviewer's role and the site; never tidy a quote.
Separate what I observed from what I infer, and begin every inference with "My read:".
Use at most two "My read:" statements in the whole document, or it turns into opinion.
What We Should Do is a numbered list of exactly three recommendations, most urgent first.
Each recommendation starts with a verb and ends with an owner team and a time frame in brackets, like "(Product, Q3)".
At least one recommendation should be something to stop doing or something not to copy.
Hold the whole teardown to 400 to 600 words; leadership reads the first screen and the last list.
No paragraph longer than three sentences.
Say what I couldn't verify in one sentence at the end of Evidence, starting "Not verified:".
Ask where they will be in a year, not only where they are; a weak product with a fast release cadence is not weak.
Use the present tense for what the product does and the past tense for what I did during the test.
Refer to our own product by name at least once, and never as "our solution" or "our platform".
Give the customer's reason for choosing them in the customer's terms, not in our positioning language.
Headings are ## only, in Title Case, and worded identically from one teardown to the next so they can be compared side by side.
Don't describe screenshots in prose; if a screen matters, say what I clicked and what came back in one sentence.
Finish the last recommendation and stop: no closing paragraph, no restated summary.
